headline: The overnight HRRR jumped back up and now shows a 1-inch hour around noon, on top of a soaking frontal band at the 7 AM high tide; the other models are steadier at 0.6–1.0 in for the wettest 3 hours.

summary.text: HRRR swung back: wettest 3 hours went from about 0.4 in (2 PM run) to about 1.4 in (11 PM run), with 1.05 in in the single hour ending at noon. RRFS went the other way, 1.1 to 0.6 in.
Wettest 3 hours: HRRR 1.37 in, ECMWF 0.99, NBM 0.79, RRFS 0.61. HRRR is now the high outlier. Consensus (HRRR ×1.25, RRFS, NBM: middle value) is 0.79 in.
Most likely water across the yards toward the garage doors (Yellow) at the peak. If HRRR's noon burst verifies, Red or Purple is possible; Red needs about 1.2 in in 3 hours.
Frontal rain about 6–10 AM, heaviest burst most likely 10 AM–2 PM, with HRRR's cell right around noon. Showers and thunderstorms return tonight (HRRR about 0.5 in near 11 PM) and Thursday morning.
7.0 ft high tide at 7:21 AM, NOAA model about 8.6 ft (≈1.5 ft surge, Coastal Flood Advisory). The Bay stays about 1 ft above normal through the midday burst. Channel is near empty now.
Cars out of the cul-de-sac and drain grates cleared before 7 AM. Keep the dashboard open late morning through early afternoon for the 1-hour burst alarm.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: A strong cold front is moving south from the North Bay, where rain began before midnight. NWS San Francisco (10:46 PM discussion) has the front crossing the Bay Area between 4 AM and 8 AM, with light to moderate rain ahead of it and isolated thunderstorms possible right along the boundary. Post-frontal showers and a better chance of thunderstorms follow tonight into Thursday morning as colder air and a surface low move in. NWS storm totals through Friday morning: 1.5–2.5 in for most of the Bay Area. Another, weaker front arrives Saturday into Sunday.

sections.title: What changed and model trends
sections.text:
The HRRR flipped again. Yesterday's 2 PM run had cut the burst to about 0.4 in for the wettest 3 hours; the 11 PM run is back to 1.37 in (noon–3 PM), driven by one very wet hour: 1.05 in in the hour ending at noon. It also shows the frontal band itself fairly wet, about 0.7 in from 7 to 10 AM, before that cell. The HRRR 15-minute feed has the same cell but somewhat weaker, about 0.6 in between 11:15 AM and 12:15 PM, so even within the HRRR the size of the burst is uncertain.

The other models did not follow it up. RRFS (4 PM run) dropped from 1.1 in to 0.61 in for the wettest 3 hours (10 AM–1 PM), with no hour above 0.24 in. NBM is 0.79 in (10 AM–1 PM) and ECMWF 0.99 in (11 AM–2 PM). GFS shows the same numbers as HRRR here because it blends in HRRR for the first hours, so it isn't an independent vote.

The dashboard's consensus (HRRR ×1.25 = 1.71, RRFS 0.61, NBM 0.79; middle value) is 0.79 in, just into Yellow. HRRR's 1.05 in hour also trips the 1-hour rule (≥ 0.40 in means at least Yellow). Given HRRR's history of under-forecasting our big bursts and the thunderstorm potential along the front, I think the consensus is a reasonable floor, not a ceiling.

Storm totals over the next 72 hours: ECMWF 3.8 in, HRRR 3.3 in (its run ends Thursday 10 PM), RRFS 2.3 in, NBM 2.2 in.

sections.title: Tide and the channel
sections.text:
Redwood City high tide is predicted at 7.0 ft (MLLW) at 7:21 AM, and NOAA's Bay model peaks near 8.6 ft around 7:30–7:45 AM, about 1.5 ft of surge. NWS has a Coastal Flood Advisory from 5 AM today to 10 AM Thursday. The frontal band arrives right at that high tide, when the Bayfront Canal and Atherton Channel drain slowest. The tide then falls toward a predicted 2.8 ft low at 1:23 PM, but the Bay model keeps it about 1 ft higher (near 4.0 ft around 2 PM), so drainage during the midday burst will be better than at dawn but not as good as a normal low tide. Thursday's high is higher: 7.4 ft predicted at 7:58 AM, with the Bay model near 9.6 ft (about 2 ft of surge), in case Thursday-morning thunderstorms bring a second burst.

Channel: Atherton Channel at Alameda de las Pulgas read 0.14 ft at midnight (Flood Monitoring is 3.18 ft). The gauge upstream of Caltrain last reported 0.07 ft at 5:13 PM Tuesday (Monitoring 2.8 ft); its feed updates infrequently, so the reading is about 8 hours old.

sections.title: Current observations
sections.text: Still dry on the street as of about 1 AM; none of the models has measurable rain here yet. Rain is under way in the North Bay and moving south. The channel is essentially empty, so the system starts with all of its capacity, but the ground is damp from earlier this week and runoff will come quickly once the rain gets going.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.text: High. The wettest-3-hour spread is 0.61 to 1.37 in, and the HRRR alone has swung from 1.4 to 0.4 and back to 1.4 in in three runs. That kind of flip-flop usually means a narrow, intense rain band or embedded storm cell whose exact track the models can't pin down; a 10–20 mile shift decides whether it hits Atherton. Any thunderstorm can drop 0.5 in in 20–30 minutes regardless of what the models show. Most likely outcome: Yellow at the peak, possibly Green if the RRFS is right. Red (about 1.2 in in 3 hours) or Purple (about 1.4 in) requires the HRRR's noon cell to verify over us. The RRFS run is now about 9 hours old; newer RRFS and HRRR runs before dawn should help.

sections.title: What to do this morning
sections.text:
• Move cars out of the cul-de-sac before about 7 AM; the frontal rain arrives at high tide and the heaviest burst may follow late morning.
• Clear leaves from the street drain grates and yard drains before 7 AM if it's safe to be outside; strong south winds overnight will bring down more leaves.
• If you use sandbags, set them before the rain starts.
• Gusty winds this morning can cause power outages. The pump station needs power; if the power goes out during heavy rain, assume the pumps may be slow and watch the street.
• Keep the dashboard open from late morning through early afternoon: the 1-hour burst alarm needs live readings.
• During the peak, take a photo of the street with the time visible.
• Don't drive or walk through moving water.
